strengths: Novel exploration of dynamic frame rates for very low frame rate (≤10Hz) neural audio codecs with strong empirical validation; demonstrating 87% relative WER improvement over DualCodec at 6.25Hz (4.15% vs 31.5%)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with proper controls: retrained baselines at equivalent frame rates, detailed ablation studies, interpretable visualization of merging patterns aligned with phonemes, and downstream task validation
Well-motivated design with clear problem articulation; strong correlation (r=0.775) between phoneme rate and frame rate convincingly demonstrates semantic alignment of dynamic merging

Technically sound architecture combining ASR features, dual-stream encoding, and Transformer refinement; demonstrated utility in TTS applications with 3.4x AR-stage speedup and competitive subjective quality
Excellent reproducibility: comprehensive implementation details, hyperparameter specifications, promise of code release, and systematic documentation of all experimental configurations
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: combines existing techniques (dual-stream from DualCodec, token merging from DynTok, FSQ quantization, Transformer bottlenecks) without significant methodological innovation; primarily an engineering contribution

Critical practical limitation: dynamic-rate tokens must be unmerged before NAR decoding, eliminating compression benefits for generative models. Direct audio generation from dynamic tokens is left as future work, severely limiting applicability to language model-based audio synthesis

Significant missing baselines: No direct comparison with TaDiCodec (6.25Hz), TASTE (≤10Hz), CodecSlime, TFC, or VARSTok despite discussing these concurrent works; only compares retrained higher-frame-rate codecs, making competitive assessment difficult

Narrow evaluation scope limited to English (LibriSpeech only) despite proposing ASR-dependent method; multilingual support deferred to future work. Generalization to other languages, accents, domains, or non-speech audio unvalidated. Empirical threshold τ selection with no principled method for domain adaptation

Modest practical advantages unclear: acoustic metrics show minimal improvement from dynamic frame rate (Table 4: PESQ/UTMOS unchanged, only marginal MCD/SIM gains). Authors acknowledge acoustic fidelity is bitrate-constrained. TTS with 12.5Hz NAR shows degraded quality (NMOS 2.87-2.93 vs 3.27-3.32); total speedup with NAR (1.4x) modest

Parameter overhead not justified: 216M trainable parameters (2.5x larger than DualCodec's 84M), with frame unmerging transformer consuming 100M alone. Cost-benefit analysis of larger model size missing

Incomplete evaluation: ASR probing task (Table 3) only evaluated for 3 configurations due to time constraints; no failure case analysis; loss function weights (5 terms) not ablated; limited subjective evaluation (6 MOS raters); no analysis of robustness to ASR quality or noisy speech

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem (low frame rate codecs for speech language models) with clear motivation and demonstrated need

Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation: retrained baselines at matched frame rates, extensive ablations (Tables 3-4, 8-9), downstream tasks (TTS, audio understanding), OOD and multilingual testing
Strong empirical results in semantic preservation (4.15% WER at 6.25Hz vs 31.5% for DualCodec) with interpretability analysis showing alignment with phonetic structure (Figure 4, r=0.775)

Practical advantages: inference-time controllable frame rates (3-12.5Hz) without retraining, low computational cost (RTF 0.018 encode/0.006 decode), and demonstrated effectiveness in downstream TTS application
Well-documented technical approach with clear presentation, promised code release, and extensive appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (dynamic merging adapted from DynTok, dual-stream from DualCodec, standard components like FSQ/Transformers) rather than introducing fundamental innovations

Strong external dependency on frozen ASR model (SenseVoice-Small) with unclear justification; only one ASR model tested despite claiming ASR is key contribution; multilingual failure directly attributable to this dependency (100% WER on unseen languages)

Overly simplistic frame merging algorithm: greedy left-to-right with fixed cosine similarity threshold, no learnable parameters, threshold τ tuned on test set risking overfitting; authors acknowledge (Appendix J) this could be improved but don't pursue it

Significant multilingual limitations: trained only on English audiobook data, zero-shot performance on unseen languages extremely poor, requires language-specific fine-tuning to be practical—limiting applicability as general-purpose codec

Frame length quantization (max 8 frames = 3 bits) hard constraint unexplored; acoustic-semantic trade-off underexplored (Table 4 shows dynamic rate helps semantics but degrades acoustic metrics like MCD/SIM)
Incomplete comparison with concurrent work: XY-Tokenizer (12.5Hz ASR-based codec) only briefly discussed in appendix; authors acknowledge concurrent approach's explicit ASR loss may be beneficial

Design choices lack deep justification: FSQ dimensions (D=5, L=8), specific ASR model choice, transformer configurations appear arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis; complex system with 216M parameters and unclear reproducibility of training stability tricks
Limited analysis of failure modes: performance degrades significantly at extreme low rates (3Hz: 51.5% WER); no investigation of content-specific failures or problematic speech types

TTS evaluation limitations: only 10 samples for human evaluation, clean speech only, comparison complicated by different NAR frame rates across systems, no comparison of generation quality versus semantic token quality

Potential test set overfitting: frame merging threshold τ tuned based on "trial runs on test set"; training stability issues mentioned (delaying parameter updates, bypassing layers) raise reproducibility concerns

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple frame rates with semantic, acoustic, and downstream task metrics
Strong empirical results on semantic preservation (4.15% WER at 6.25Hz), notably outperforming retrained baselines on RVQ-1 metrics
Interpretable analysis showing dynamic frame rate alignment with phonemic structure (Figure 4-5)
Well-designed architecture with clear technical motivation for dual-stream encoding and frame merging/unmerging modules
Extensive ablation studies validating design choices
Practical inference-time controllability across frame rates (3-12.5Hz)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: dynamic frame rate merging already exists in CodecSlime, TFC, VARSTok; the primary contribution is using ASR features instead of other similarity metrics, which is incremental

Weak and self-contradicted motivation: the core premise that lower AR frame rates benefit downstream tasks is undermined by Table 6 (TTS results), where 6.25Hz AR performs similarly to or better than 12.5Hz AR
Acoustic quality metrics (PESQ, MCD, UTMOS, SIM) show minimal improvement with dynamic frame rate (Tables 3-4), suggesting benefits are limited to semantic tokens only

Methodological concerns: (1) test-set contamination via threshold τ tuning on test split; (2) unfair baseline comparisons (DAC/DualCodec retraining may be suboptimal); (3) confounded TTS comparison mixing codec quality with AR frame rate effects
Critical dependence on frozen SenseVoice-Small ASR model: Table 8 shows 6.6× WER gap across ASR models (27.3% vs 4.15%), raising generalization concerns
Fundamental architectural limitation (footnote 2): dynamic frame rates only apply to encoding, not end-to-end generation, as NAR decoder requires fixed 12.5Hz input
Overstated claims: 'among the first codecs below 10Hz' when TaDiCodec (6.25Hz) and TASTE (≤10Hz) already exist; concurrent work (CodecSlime, XY-Tokenizer) not sufficiently differentiated
No theoretical justification for why ASR features are superior to SSL features beyond empirical observation
Multilingual capability severely limited: zero-shot performance on unseen languages is poor (50-100% WER), requiring language-specific fine-tuning
Presentation obscures core contributions: 27-page main paper with extensive appendices makes it difficult to identify what is fundamentally novel
Modest correlation (r=0.775) between phoneme rate and frame rate (Figure 4) does not strongly validate the semantic complexity adaptation claim

strengths: Novel dynamic frame rate mechanism for <10Hz audio codecs addressing real computational bottleneck in speech language models
Dramatic semantic preservation improvements at very low frame rates (4.15% WER at 6.25Hz vs 31.5% for DualCodec)
Strong interpretability: FlexiCodec frame rate correlates with phoneme rate (r=0.775), aligning merging patterns with linguistic units
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across semantic/acoustic metrics, downstream TTS, audio understanding tasks, and OOD/multilingual data
Thorough ablation studies and factorial analysis clearly isolating contributions of each component (Tables 3-4, 8-9)
Practical utility demonstrated with significant speedups (7.3× in TTS AR stage) while maintaining competitive quality
Good reproducibility with detailed implementation details, configurations, and code release planned
Well-motivated problem addressing gap between 50Hz+ audio codecs and ~4.5Hz text representation
weaknesses: Incremental contribution building on existing dual-stream codecs and borrowing token merging from vision domain without major conceptual breakthroughs
Acoustic quality improvements modest compared to semantic gains (PESQ/MCD/SIM improvements small over DualCodec; 2.76 PESQ at 6.25Hz vs 4.5 ground truth)
Dependency on frozen 230M parameter ASR model (450M total including frozen weights) and multilingual limitations requiring language-specific finetuning (Table 12)
Simple greedy left-to-right frame merging algorithm without learnable parameters; unclear if globally optimal versus locally reasonable solution
Streaming not supported—operates only in full-utterance mode, limiting applicability for real-time speech applications despite being acknowledged need
Limited analysis of baseline comparisons with concurrent dynamic-rate methods (CodecSlime, TFC, VARSTok) and XY-Tokenizer relegated to appendix
TTS experimental results incremental—MOS scores competitive but not exceptional (3.27-3.32 NMOS) and quality degrades noticeably with 12.5Hz NAR
No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or error analysis of failure modes and challenging speech types
Asymmetric quantization schemes (FSQ for semantic, RVQ for acoustic) not fully justified; rFSQ exploration relegated to future work
Evaluation primarily on clean LibriSpeech data with limited exploration of highly noisy or spontaneous speech performance
